Hmm, the key here is to determine how many times each locker is toggled. Because each toggle changes the state of the locker—opening it if it's closed, closing it if it's open. So, if a locker is toggled an odd number of times, it will end up open. If it's toggled an even number of times, it'll end up closed.

Now, why does the number of toggles matter? Well, each locker is toggled by the students whose numbers are divisors of the locker's number. For example, locker number 6 is toggled by student 1 (since 1 divides 6), student 2 (2 divides 6), student 3 (3 divides 6), and student 6 (6 divides 6). So, locker 6 is toggled 4 times. Since 4 is even, it would end up closed.

Perfect squares have an odd number of divisors because one of the divisors is repeated. For example, locker number 9 is toggled by students 1, 3, and 9. That's three times, which is odd. So locker 9 would be open.

So, the conclusion is that lockers which are perfect squares will be open at the end because they have an odd number of divisors, leading to an odd number of toggles, which changes the state from closed to open. All other lockers have an even number of divisors, so they end up closed.

Locker 10: toggled by 1, 2, 5, 10 (4 times) → closed.
